```{r a1-setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 120, out.width = "100%")
options(width = 82)
```

This article grades six sites whose scores are uncertain. A full ranking
puts every pair of sites in order, even when the data leave their order
uncertain. `postrank()` can instead place two sites in the same integer grade,
which leaves that pair unordered. The chosen grading balances two posterior
expected costs: reporting a pair in the wrong order, and leaving a pair
unordered.

We first grade the sites on one criterion (one score), then add a second
criterion so all six sites receive one common grading across both scores.
Grade 1 is the highest priority. Sites in different grades are reported in
that order. Sites in the same grade are left unordered; this does not mean
that their scores are equal.

## The example sites {#begin-with-a-small-posterior-input}

```{r a1-load}
library(postrank)
sites <- pr_tutorial
```

The example has six fictional sites, `A` through `F`. Each site's score has a
normal posterior distribution with standard deviation `0.2`, in illustrative
standardized units. Sites are independent, and so are the two scores within
each site. Larger score values mean higher priority on both criteria. These
distributions are synthetic and were created for teaching rather than fitted
to observations from real sites.

`sites$one` holds the first criterion (`score_A`), and `sites$two` holds both
criteria (`score_A` and `score_B`, with the same distribution for `score_A`).
For any two sites, the pairwise comparison probability is the posterior
probability that one site's score exceeds the other's. Because the tutorial
distributions are normal, those comparison probabilities and the marginal
posterior intervals follow analytically from the means and standard
deviations, and `pr_tutorial` stores them directly. When you analyze output
from your own model (such as Stan, brms, or JAGS), you first build an input
describing each criterion, its priority direction, and how the draws were
generated; see
[Preparing your posterior draws and comparison probabilities](a5-your-posterior-results.html).

```{r a1-law}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Site = sites$units$label, sites$law$means),
  row.names = FALSE, digits = 2,
  col.names = c("Site", "Score A mean", "Score B mean"))
```

## Choosing `tau` and `G_max` on one criterion {#choose-what-the-first-report-should-say}

Two policy settings shape a one-criterion grading:

- `G_max = 3` allows at most three distinct grades (fewer grades are also
  allowed if they give lower loss).
- `tau = 0.2` is the cost of leaving a pair unordered, relative to cost `1`
  for reporting a pair in the wrong order (`0 < tau <= 0.5`).

The loss is the posterior expected cost averaged over all `M` unordered pairs
of sites. Considered one pair at a time, ordering a pair has lower expected
cost than leaving it unordered only when its more likely direction has
posterior probability above `1 - tau` (here `0.8`). Because integer grades
must be transitive across all pairs and `G_max` caps the number of grades,
the optimal grading can differ from that pair-by-pair rule. Smaller values of
`tau` make unordered pairs cheaper and tend to order fewer pairs. With one
criterion, `weights` defaults to `1`.

Computing a grading requires an optimization solver: Gurobi is the default
and requires a Gurobi license, or you can install the open-source HiGHS
solver with `install.packages("highs")` and pass `backend = "highs"`. The
chunk below shows the solver call without running it (`eval = FALSE`), and
the next chunk loads the stored result from an equivalent call with
`postrank_example()`:

```{r a1-one-call, eval=FALSE}
one <- postrank(sites$one, tau = 0.2, G_max = 3, backend = "highs",
  control = postrank_control(time_limit = 60, threads = 1, seed = 1304))
```

```{r a1-one-result}
one <- postrank_example("tutorial_one")
one
```

In the printed output, "disclosed" pairs are the ordered pairs, "withheld"
pairs are the unordered pairs, and "risk" is the posterior expected loss. The
solver also reports a lower bound (a loss no valid grading can beat) and a
gap (the returned grading's loss minus that lower bound). Here the warning
notes that floating-point solver tolerances placed the raw lower bound
slightly above the checked grading's loss ("validated action risk", where
"action" means the grading), so `postrank` clamped the bound to the loss and
recorded gap `0`; see
[Computing grades, choosing settings, and reading solver bounds](m5-computing-grades.html)
for details. The report card was prepared; Monte Carlo fragility was not,
because `sites$one` supplies analytic normal distributions rather than
posterior draws.

The grading uses `3` grades and orders `12` of the `15` site pairs (`80.0%`),
leaving `3` pairs unordered. Sites `A` and `B` are in grade 1, `C` and `D` in
grade 2, and `E` and `F` in grade 3. Because `A` is in grade 1 and `C` is in
grade 2, the report places `A` above `C`. Because `A` and `B` share grade 1,
that pair is left unordered; listing `A` before `B` within grade 1 carries no
order.

We can read the error counts and recompute the loss directly from the
exported accessors:

```{r a1-risk}
p <- get_profile(one)
rel <- get_relations(one)
M <- sum(upper.tri(rel))
N <- sum(rel[upper.tri(rel)] != 0L)
p[, c("criterion", "E", "E_over_N", "risk")]
c(recomputed = (p$E + one$settings$tau * (M - N)) / M,
  stored = get_risk(one)$risk)
```

Among the `N = 12` ordered pairs, the posterior expected number of
wrong-direction pairs is `E =` `r round(p$E, 4)`, or `E / N =`
`r round(p$E_over_N, 4)` expected wrong-direction errors per ordered pair (an
average across the `12` ordered pairs, each of which has its own error
probability). Adding the `M - N = 3` unordered pairs at cost `tau = 0.2` each
and dividing by all `M = 15` pairs gives the overall loss
`r round(get_risk(one)$risk, 4)`. Placing all six sites in a single grade
would leave all `15` pairs unordered, giving loss `tau = 0.2` and `E / N = NA`
because zero pairs are ordered.

`summary(one)` prints the settings, solver status, lower bound, gap, and
warnings together. Those solver quantities describe optimization over the
supplied comparison probabilities, not uncertainty in the site scores or
whether the normal model fits real data.

## Reading marginal intervals alongside grades {#read-estimates-alongside-grades}

```{r a1-one-card, fig.cap="Score A posterior means and 90% equal-tail marginal intervals for the six fictional sites, grouped by their assigned grades.", fig.alt="Horizontal dot-and-interval report card for six sites on Score A, grouped into grade 1 (A, B), grade 2 (C, D), and grade 3 (E, F)."}
postrank_plot_report_card(one,
  entity_labels = setNames(sites$units$label, sites$units$entity_id),
  criterion_labels = c(score_A = "Score A (standardized units)"))
```

Each dot and horizontal bar shows the posterior mean and 90% equal-tail
marginal interval for one site's score, taken one site at a time, while the
grade panels show which site pairs are ordered and which are left unordered.
These bars are marginal intervals for the continuous scores rather than
simultaneous bands across all six sites or intervals for the integer grades.
Overlapping score intervals can occur across grades. The grades come from
the pairwise comparison probabilities together with `tau` and `G_max`
(`plot(one)` draws the default report card without custom axis labels).
You can extract the two-column grade table with `as.data.frame(one)`, the
report-card interval table with `as.data.frame(one, what = "report_card")`,
and the named grade vector with `get_grades(one)`.

## Adding a second criterion {#add-a-second-criterion}

Next we include `score_B`. Sites `C` and `D` have lower `score_A` means than
`B` (`0.25` and `0.15` versus `0.95`), whereas their `score_B` means (`0.90`
and `0.60`) exceed `B`'s (`0.40`). Requiring one common grading across both
criteria means every site pair gets a single order decision that balances
errors on both scores. Here we give equal weights (`0.5` and `0.5`) to the
two criteria and keep `tau = 0.2` and `G_max = 3`.

As before, the solver call is shown with `eval = FALSE`, and we load the
stored result from an equivalent call with `postrank_example()`:

```{r a1-two-call, eval=FALSE}
two <- postrank(sites$two,
  weights = c(score_A = 0.5, score_B = 0.5),
  tau = 0.2, G_max = 3, backend = "highs",
  control = postrank_control(time_limit = 60, threads = 1, seed = 1304))
```

```{r a1-two-result}
two <- postrank_example("tutorial_two")
as.data.frame(two)
p2 <- get_profile(two)
p2[, c("criterion", "weight", "E", "E_over_N", "risk")]
get_risk(two)$risk
```

```{r a1-two-counts}
rel2 <- get_relations(two)
c(ordered = sum(rel2[upper.tri(rel2)] != 0L),
  unordered = sum(rel2[upper.tri(rel2)] == 0L))
```

The common grading places sites `A`, `B`, `C`, and `D` together in grade 1,
`E` in grade 2, and `F` in grade 3. It orders `9` of the `15` pairs and
leaves `6` pairs unordered (all six pairs among `A` through `D`), with
weighted two-criterion loss `r round(get_risk(two)$risk, 4)`. Even with equal
weights, the expected wrong-direction errors per ordered pair differ across
criteria (`r round(p2$E_over_N[1], 4)` on `score_A` and
`r round(p2$E_over_N[2], 4)` on `score_B`): `weights` weight each criterion's
expected errors in the objective rather than forcing equal error rates.

```{r a1-two-card, fig.height=4.8, fig.cap="Posterior means and 90% equal-tail marginal intervals for Score A and Score B across the six sites under one common grading.", fig.alt="Two-panel horizontal dot-and-interval report card for Score A and Score B, sharing grades 1 (A, B, C, D), 2 (E), and 3 (F)."}
postrank_plot_report_card(two,
  entity_labels = setNames(sites$units$label, sites$units$entity_id),
  criterion_labels = c(score_A = "Score A (standardized units)",
    score_B = "Score B (standardized units)"))
```

The grouping changes from `2 / 2 / 2` to `4 / 1 / 1` because the grading now
accounts for `score_B` while `score_A`'s posterior distribution is unchanged.
Do not compare `one`'s one-criterion loss (`r round(get_risk(one)$risk, 4)`)
directly with `two`'s two-criterion loss (`r round(get_risk(two)$risk, 4)`):
they average over different sets of criteria. To compare candidate gradings,
evaluate them on the same posterior input, weights, and `tau` using
`postrank_evaluate()` or `postrank_compare()`.
